title: Ramberg–Bäcklund reaction
subtitle: An α-chloro sulfone and base: an episulfone loses SO₂ to give an alkene

reactants.caption: 1-chloroethyl ethyl sulfone + potassium hydroxide
reactants.learnerPrompt: Make a carbanion that can reach the C–Cl carbon.
hintTiers: A sulfonyl group makes the hydrogens next to it acidic. The carbanion you want must be able to attack the carbon carrying chlorine, so which side of the sulfone should lose a proton?
Hydroxide takes the drawn hydrogen on the side without chlorine; the C–H pair stays on that carbon. Two arrows.
Hydroxide lone pair → new bond to the drawn H; that C–H bond → a lone pair on its carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Halides next to a sulfonyl group are very poor at SN2 reactions with external nucleophiles. Hydroxide acts as a base here.

carbanion.caption: the α-sulfonyl carbanion + water
carbanion.learnerPrompt: The carbanion displaces chloride. Draw the ring closure.
hintTiers: The carbanion and the C–Cl carbon are both bonded to sulfur. If they bond to each other, how big is the ring?
The carbanion bonds to the carbon carrying chlorine, and the C–Cl pair leaves with chloride. Two arrows: a three-membered ring with sulfur in it.
Carbanion lone pair → new bond to the carbon carrying chlorine; C–Cl bond → a lone pair on chlorine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Taking the proton back from water just returns to the start. The carbanion has a better reaction inside the molecule.

episulfone.caption: the episulfone (a thiirane 1,1-dioxide) + chloride
episulfone.learnerPrompt: The episulfone falls apart. Draw the loss of sulfur dioxide.
hintTiers: The three-membered ring is strained, and SO₂ is a very stable gas. Which two bonds break, and where does the C=C bond form?
Both C–S bonds break: the pair of one becomes the new C=C π bond and the pair of the other stays on sulfur, as SO₂ leaves. Two arrows.
One C–S bond → C=C π bond between the two ring carbons; the other C–S bond → a lone pair on sulfur.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: No nucleophile is needed: the strained episulfone breaks up on its own, losing SO₂.

products.caption: but-2-ene + sulfur dioxide + potassium chloride + water

steps.explanationAfterStep: Hydroxide removes a proton next to the sulfonyl group, on the side without chlorine. (Deprotonation on the chlorine side also happens, but that carbanion cannot cyclise and is simply reprotonated.)
The carbanion displaces chloride inside the molecule, an intramolecular SN2 reaction: a three-membered episulfone forms.

Both C–S bonds break in one step (a cheletropic extrusion): SO₂ leaves and the C=C bond forms where the ring was. With aqueous hydroxide the Z-alkene is often the major isomer. The app does not check E/Z geometry yet.

mechanismSummary: Hydroxide removes a proton next to the sulfonyl group on the side without chlorine. The carbanion displaces chloride inside the molecule, giving a three-membered episulfone. This loses SO₂ in one concerted step, and a C=C bond forms where the two carbons were joined through sulfur. Overall the sulfone is cut out and the two carbons on either side become an alkene: but-2-ene.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 27
